evidence: This is supported by in vitro cell viability data and a citation to literature on Liproxstatin-1.

claim: Ferroptotic cell death was mainly described in genetic models with disturbed detoxification of lipid peroxides due to conditional loss of Gpx4.
source: Thus far ferroptotic cell death was mainly described in genetic models, for example with disturbed detoxification of lipid peroxides due to conditional loss of Gpx4 (Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Matsushita et al., 2015) or in various pathologies (Park et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ferroptosis may critically contribute to RPM loss during physiological aging.
source: Here, we propose that ferroptosis may critically contribute to RPM loss during physiological aging.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing ferroptosis markers in aged RPMs and rescue by ferroptosis inhibitors.

claim: Excessive clearance of damaged RBCs in mouse models causes transient or sustained RPM depletion.
source: Notably, the excessive clearance of damaged RBCs in mouse models of blood transfusion, hemolytic anemia, or the anemia of inflammation induced by heat-killed Brucella abortus was previously shown to cause transient or sustained RPMs depletion (Haldar et al., 2014; Theurl et al., 2016; Youssef et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The splenic niche may be replenished to some extent via splenic monocyte recruitment and/or resident RPMs proliferation.
source: Although the splenic niche may be replenished to some extent via splenic monocyte recruitment and/or resident RPMs proliferation (Haldar et al., 2014; Youssef et al., 2018), our data imply that the damage of embryonically derived RPM in these models may lead to the irreversible formation of insoluble iron-rich splenic protein aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The damage of embryonically derived RPMs may lead to the irreversible formation of insoluble iron-rich splenic protein aggregates.
source: Although the splenic niche may be replenished to some extent via splenic monocyte recruitment and/or resident RPMs proliferation (Haldar et al., 2014; Youssef et al., 2018), our data imply that the damage of embryonically derived RPM in these models may lead to the irreversible formation of insoluble iron-rich splenic protein aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing aggregate formation in aged mice and after iron dextran injection.

claim: Thalassemic mice display enhanced splenic Perls'-stained deposits that appear to be extracellular and are not amenable to iron chelation therapy.
source: However, interestingly, thalassemic mice display enhanced splenic Perls'-stained deposits that appear to be extracellular and are not amenable to iron chelation therapy (Sanyear et al., 2020; Vadolas et al., 2021), possibly resembling those identified by the present study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on thalassemic mice.

claim: Genetic disruption of Hrg1 leads to the formation of heme aggregate hemozoin inside enlarged phagolysosomes.
source: Of note, genetic disruption of Hrg1 leads to the formation of heme aggregate hemozoin inside enlarged phagolysosomes (Pek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Iron accumulation in RPMs, independently of ROS generation, is a major driver of erythrophagocytosis suppression during aging, likely via the downregulation of apoptotic cell receptors and calcium signaling.
source: Among them, iron accumulation in RPMs, independently of ROS generation, emerged as a major driver of EP suppression during aging, likely via the downregulation of apoptotic cell receptors (Slusarczyk and Mleczko-Sanecka, 2021) and calcium signaling (Ma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by data showing that iron reduction but not NAC rescues EP, and by data showing downregulation of receptors and calcium upon iron loading, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Iron loading decreases the capacity of RPMs for phagolysosomal RBC degradation.
source: We also demonstrated that iron loading decreases the capacity of RPMs for phagolysosomal RBC degradation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing decreased lysosomal activity upon iron loading.

claim: Patients with Gaucher disease show iron deposits in the splenic macrophages.
source: Of note, patients who suffer from lysosomal storage disorder, Gaucher disease, show iron deposits in the splenic macrophages (Clarke et al., 2021; Lefebvre et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Iron sequestration in Gaucher macrophages was attributed to hepcidin-mediated downregulation of ferroportin, or more recently to increased erythrophagocytosis of Gaucher RBCs.
source: Iron sequestration in Gaucher macrophages was attributed to the hepcidin-mediated downregulation of ferroportin, or more recently to increased erythrophagocytosis of Gaucher RBCs (Dupuis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: Defects in proteostasis, due to defective lysosomal-mediated protein quality control, may contribute to aberrant iron management in Gaucher macrophages.
source: Based on our study, it is plausible that defects in proteostasis, due to defective lysosomal-mediated protein quality control, may contribute to aberrant iron management in Gaucher macrophages.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the current study showing links between lysosomal defects, proteostasis, and iron management.

claim: HO-1 is well characterized for its cytoprotective, anti-oxidative, and anti-inflammatory functions.
source: HO-1 is well characterized for its cytoprotective, anti-oxidative, and anti-inflammatory functions, (Gozzelino et al., 2010), and its activity was proposed to prevent cellular senescence (Even et al., 2018; Hedblom et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2018; Suliman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HO-1 activity was proposed to prevent cellular senescence.
source: HO-1 is well characterized for its cytoprotective, anti-oxidative, and anti-inflammatory functions, (Gozzelino et al., 2010), and its activity was proposed to prevent cellular senescence (Even et al., 2018; Hedblom et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2018; Suliman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RPMs are key cells where HO-1 exerts its enzymatic function.
source: Since RPMs are key cells where HO-1 exerts its enzymatic function (Vijayan et al., 2018), our observation that HO-1 levels decrease in these cells during aging is of high physiological significance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The suppression of erythrophagocytosis by inhibition of HO-1 activity may be mediated by heme overload.
source: The suppression of EP by inhibition of HO-1 activity may be mediated by heme overload, as shown previously for general phagocytosis (Martins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CO administration protects Hmox1 knock-out mice from sepsis-induced lethality via stimulation of bacterial phagocytosis.
source: These findings are in agreement with the previous work, reporting that CO administration protects Hmox1 knock-out mice from sepsis-induced lethality via stimulation of bacterial phagocytosis (Chung et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Intracellular iron loading of RPMs impairs their erythrophagocytosis capacity.
source: Collectively, our study implies that intracellular iron loading of RPMs impairs their EP capacity and synergistically with proteostasis defects leads to their demise.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental data showing reduced EP upon iron loading.

claim: Intracellular iron loading of RPMs synergistically with proteostasis defects leads to their demise.
source: Collectively, our study implies that intracellular iron loading of RPMs impairs their EP capacity and synergistically with proteostasis defects leads to their demise.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro data showing cytotoxicity only when iron loading and proteotoxic stress are combined.

claim: RPM impairments result in local RBC dyshomeostasis in the spleen, due to the shift from phagocytosis to splenic RBC lysis.
source: These impairments result in local RBC dyshomeostasis in the spleen, due to the shift from phagocytosis to splenic RBC lysis (Klei et al., 2020), and the formation of extracellular proteinaceous aggregates, rich in iron and heme, emerging from damaged RPMs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced EP, increased splenic RBC ROS, and increased extracellular heme, with a citation to literature on splenic RBC lysis.

claim: The build-up of un-degradable iron-rich particles, in concert with increased hepcidin levels, and limited iron-recycling activity of the remaining RPMs limit plasma iron availability during aging.
source: We propose that the build-up of un-degradable iron-rich particles, in concert with increased hepcidin levels, and limited iron-recycling activity of the remaining RPMs limit plasma iron availability during aging.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing aggregate formation, increased hepcidin, reduced EP, and decreased transferrin saturation.

claim: Microglia iron overload and ferroptosis were recently identified as critical drivers of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Interestingly, microglia iron overload and ferroptosis were recently identified as critical drivers of neurodegenerative diseases (Kenkhuis et al., 2021; Ryan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Long-term reduction of dietary iron intake may represent an alternative for neurodegeneration prevention.
source: In such context, our findings suggest that in addition to various iron chelation approaches (Liu et al., 2018), long-term reduction of dietary iron intake may represent an alternative for neurodegeneration prevention.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings showing benefits of dietary iron reduction in RPMs and a citation to literature on iron chelation.

claim: The degree of RPM collapse depends on dietary iron and internal hepcidin-ferroportin regulatory circuitry.
source: Having established that the degree of RPM collapse depends on dietary iron and internal hepcidin-ferroportin regulatory circuitry, it remains to be investigated how it is manifested in male mice on iron-rich genetic backgrounds or humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing rescue of RPM phenotypes by dietary iron reduction and the role of hepcidin-ferroportin axis.

claim: Standard mouse diets contain more-than-sufficient amounts of iron.
source: Lastly, since standard mouse diets contain more-than-sufficient amounts of iron, our study could be also interpreted as the effect of long-term exposure to excessive iron on RPM functions.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of standard mouse diet composition.
